records.sourceFile: Prevalence of cardiovascular disease and risk factors among former National Football League players.pdf

paper.citation: Okoh AK, Amponsah MKD, Cheffet-Walsh S, Patel M, Carfagno D, Linton D, et al. Prevalence of Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Factors Among Former National Football League Players. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;83(19):1827-1837.
paper.abstract: HUDDLE was a multicity cross-sectional study of NFL alumni and family members aged 50 and over who had health history reporting, blood pressure, ECG and transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) screening, with a 30-day follow-up call. This report covers the former NFL players, estimates the prevalence of hypertension and structural cardiac abnormalities, and tests hypertension as a predictor of abnormal TTE findings.
paper.tldr: In 285 former NFL players aged 50 and over, hypertension was found at screening in 89.8% although only 37.5% reported it, and 61.8% had structural cardiac abnormalities on echocardiography. Screening hypertension was associated with these abnormalities, but the study has no comparison group and no outcome follow-up.
paper.methods: Players were recruited through NFL Alumni Association chapters and screened at 9 events in 8 US cities between August 2021 and August 2022. Each participant completed a self-reported health history, blood pressure readings, a 12-lead ECG and a TTE, read by a central core lab, and a physician follow-up call at 30 days. Hypertension was defined as a reported history, medication use, or a screening reading of 130/80 mm Hg or higher, and multivariable logistic regression was used to identify predictors of structural abnormality on TTE.
paper.findings: Hypertension prevalence was 89.8% (255 of 284), and 81.5% (145 of 178) of players without a reported history had a screening BP of 130/80 mm Hg or higher. Structural abnormalities on TTE were present in 61.8% of the 285 evaluable players, and 46.1% had abnormal ECG findings. In the multivariable model, hypertension at screening was associated with structural abnormalities on TTE (OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.03 to 3.96; P=0.04), and investigators recommended further follow-up for 76.7% (207 of the 270 players with follow-up reasons recorded).
paper.limitations: The study was sponsored by Edwards Lifesciences, which funded it, organised the screening events, collected health histories and was involved in study design, data management and statistical analyses; nine authors are sponsor employees and others report consulting, proctoring or grants from the sponsor. In the multivariable model abnormal ECG was borderline (OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.82, P=0.05), and the authors report it as no longer significant. Self-report, volunteer recruitment through alumni chapters, no comparison group, mainly southern US sites, clinician-judged follow-up and no long-term outcomes all limit generalisation.
paper.practicalImplications: For former players aged 50 and over, the study supports checking blood pressure at routine contact, because hypertension was common in this sample and largely unreported beforehand. Players with hypertension may benefit from echocardiographic assessment, since hypertension was associated with structural abnormalities in this sample, but the study does not show that screening improves outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: The study covers former players and does not address training, performance or active players. Its relevance to current athletes is limited to the idea that hypertension and cardiac remodelling can occur in athletes and persist after retirement.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to sport or return to play. Its findings about elevated blood pressure and structural abnormalities in retired players do not establish clearance criteria for active players.

records.sourceFile: Prevalence of illness, poor mental health and sleep quality and low energy availability prior to the 2016 Summer Olympic Games.pdf

paper.citation: Drew M, Vlahovich N, Hughes D, Appaneal R, Burke LM, Lundy B, et al. Prevalence of illness, poor mental health and sleep quality and low energy availability prior to the 2016 Summer Olympic Games. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52:1-8.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional study of Australian Olympic athletes from 11 sports, surveyed about 3 months before the 2016 Rio Olympic Games. It estimates the prevalence of illness symptoms, sleep quality, mental health symptoms, low energy availability and stress-recovery state, and their associations with recent illness.
paper.tldr: In 132 Australian Olympic athletes surveyed 3 months before Rio 2016, 49% had poor sleep quality, 40% of LEAF-Q responses were above the low energy availability cut-off, and low energy availability was associated with several self-reported illness symptoms. Symptoms were self-reported at one time point, so these are associations and not causes.
paper.methods: Athletes from 11 sports were invited to complete questionnaires between 20 April and 31 May 2016, about 3 months before the Games, covering illness and injury, depression, anxiety and stress (DASS-21), resilience, recovery-stress (REST-Q), sleep (PSQI and Epworth), low energy availability (LEAF-Q), probiotic use and travel. Associations between each health domain and recent illness were estimated as odds ratios with attributable fractions, and exploratory factor analyses were run on the questionnaire scores.
paper.findings: Of 206 athletes who consented (from an estimated 317 eligible), 132 had sufficient data (47 men aged 25.8 years and 85 women aged 24.3 years). In the previous month, 46% reported upper respiratory symptoms, 36% fatigue and 20% bodily aches, 49% had poor sleep quality on the PSQI, and 14% to 19% screened positive for depression, anxiety or stress. In Table 4, low energy availability was associated with upper respiratory symptoms (OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.3 to 12), bodily aches (OR 5.8, 1.6 to 24), gastrointestinal symptoms (OR 3.8, 1.3 to 12) and head symptoms (OR 4.4, 1.4 to 14), and the Results report poor sleep quality as associated only with gastrointestinal symptoms (OR 2.8, 1.2 to 6.9).
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional and was analysed as a case-control with no healthy controls, so no causal inference is possible, all data are self-reported, and 74 of the 206 consenting athletes had no health data (the abstract's 42% response rate is 132 of 317; the Results give 65% for consent). The text and tables disagree in places: the abstract gives the upper respiratory OR interval as 1.2 to 12 (Table 4 and Results: 1.3 to 12); Table 4 shows significant PSQI with upper respiratory symptoms (OR 2.8) and probiotic use with fatigue (OR 3.6, 1.5 to 8.5) that the Results do not mention, and the upper respiratory and gastrointestinal columns of Table 4 are identical in every row, which suggests a table error; and the LEAF-Q row (36 of 90 responses) exceeds the 85 women analysed. The LEAF-Q is validated in endurance athletes and dancers, not Summer Olympic sports.
paper.practicalImplications: Preparation-period screening for female athletes can include a low energy availability questionnaire, with a positive result prompting individual nutrition and training review rather than a diagnosis. Sleep quality is worth screening because poor sleep was common, although apart from gastrointestinal symptoms it was not associated with illness, and the study does not show that acting on any of these screens reduces illness.
paper.athleteDev: The paper addresses illness and health in the run-up to competition rather than performance, and the authors note that illness can lead to training modification and affect performance outcomes. Performance staff can use the low energy availability association as a reason to monitor nutrition and training load in female athletes, but the study has no performance data.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest the patterns may inform return-to-sport decisions, and they estimate illness symptoms last about 2 to 7 days. The study has no return-to-sport outcomes and no data on recovery after illness, so it cannot set return criteria.
